overview: One of the most important distinctions in research methodology: two variables moving together does not mean one causes the other.
genZNote: Correlation: they show up together. Causation: one actually made the other show up.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: A statistical association where two variables change together, without implying that one causes the other.
aspects.valueB: A relationship where a change in one variable directly produces a change in another.

aspects.label: What It Establishes
aspects.valueA: Only that a relationship or pattern exists between variables.
aspects.valueB: That one variable is a direct cause of change in another, typically established through controlled experimentation.

aspects.label: Confounding Variables
aspects.valueA: Can arise purely from a third, unmeasured confounding variable affecting both.
aspects.valueB: Requires ruling out confounders, reverse causation, and chance to be confidently established.

aspects.label: How It Is Established
aspects.valueA: Observational studies, statistical measures such as correlation coefficients.
aspects.valueB: Randomized controlled trials, or Bradford Hill-type criteria (strength, consistency, temporality, dose-response) in observational settings.

aspects.label: Classic Example
aspects.valueA: Ice cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer (confounded by heat/season).
aspects.valueB: Smoking causing lung cancer, established through extensive controlled and longitudinal evidence.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Variables move together, no implication of a causal link.
aspects.valueB: One variable directly produces a change in the other.

overlay.commonMisconception: "Correlation does not imply causation" is one of the most important — and most often ignored — rules in interpreting scientific data.
